passage: When the Pune school merged Class 9A and 9C for the science fair, Irawati Ma'am hoped the old rivalry would fade. It didn't. The head of department had named only 9A students as team leaders, with 9C as "helpers." Within a week the 9A kids joked that 9C couldn't wire a bulb, and 9C sat in a silent block at the back. Asif, from 9C, stopped coming to the lab at all. Irawati watched and saw what was wrong: same room, no common aim, one side in charge. She went to the principal. Together they reshuffled everything: mixed teams of four, two from each section, rotating leaders, one prize per team. The principal announced it at assembly. By the fair, Asif was explaining his team's solar oven to the judges, with a 9A boy holding the chart and nodding.

qa.q: What did the head of department name only 9A students as?
qa.a: Team leaders.

qa.q: How did Irawati Ma'am feel after watching the first week, and what did she realise?
qa.a: She was likely disappointed that the rivalry hadn't faded, and realised that the same room with no common aim and one side in charge was making it worse.

qa.q: What choices did Irawati Ma'am and the principal make, and why did they help?
qa.a: They made mixed teams of four with rotating leaders and one prize per team, announced at assembly, so students worked as equals toward a shared goal with backing from the top.

qa.q: What was the first week like for Asif, and what had changed for him by the fair?
qa.a: As a 'helper' mocked by 9A, Asif felt pushed out and stopped coming; by the fair he was explaining his team's solar oven with a 9A partner beside him.

grounding: A teacher sees that mixing rival sections with unequal roles and no shared aim hardens stereotypes, then gets equal teams, a common goal and the principal's backing.

passage: "You look like you've swallowed a lemon, Himani." Pallavi pushed a cup of tea across the staffroom table. "The friendship day with the other school. Disaster." "What happened?" "We put our girls and their girls in one hall for an hour. No task, just 'mingle.' Ours sat on one side, theirs on the other. Then one of ours said their school didn't even have a proper lab, and it got nasty." "So mixing made it worse." "Mixing like that did. Nobody had a reason to need anyone. And our girls were introduced as the 'hosts', as if they were doing them a favour." "What would you do instead?" Himani set down her cup. "Mixed teams, a real job, a heritage walk they plan together, equal roles. And both principals standing there saying it matters." "Write it up. I'll sign it."

qa.q: How long were the two schools' girls put in one hall?
qa.a: An hour.

qa.q: Why does Himani think the friendship day failed?
qa.a: Himani thinks nobody had a reason to need anyone, and calling one side 'hosts' made it unequal, so the contact only hardened the split.

qa.q: What does Himani plan instead, and why should it work better?
qa.a: Mixed teams planning a heritage walk together with equal roles and both principals backing it, so students work as equals toward a shared aim.

qa.q: How might the visiting school's girls have felt being treated as guests receiving a favour?
qa.a: They may have felt looked down on and defensive, which made the remark about the lab cut deeper and kept them on their side of the hall.

grounding: A teacher sees that bringing two schools' students together with no shared task and unequal status hardens stereotypes, and plans equal teams with a common aim and authority backing.

passage: I'm Irfan, and I've coached the school football team for three years. My worst idea came last spring. The boarders and the day scholars had been sniping at each other for months, so I made them share one practice. But I let the boarders play the match while the day scholars ran drills on the side. Within a week, Pooja, one of my best day-scholar players, was calling the boarders "the rich kids," and they were calling her lot "the bus crowd." I'd put them on the same field and made it worse. So I changed three things. Every team got an equal mix. Every drill needed both groups to score. And the principal came to watch, which told everyone this mattered. By June, Pooja was passing to a boarder for the winning goal, and nobody was keeping count of who was who.

qa.q: What did the day scholars do while the boarders played the match?
qa.a: They ran drills on the side.

qa.q: What did Irfan realise after a week of shared practice?
qa.a: Irfan realised that putting the groups on the same field with unequal roles had made the rivalry worse, not better.

qa.q: Which three changes did Irfan make, and why did they work?
qa.a: Equal mixes on every team, drills needing both groups to score, and the principal watching; together they gave equal status, a shared goal and visible backing.

qa.q: How might Pooja's view of the boarders have changed by June?
qa.a: From 'the rich kids' to teammates she could trust with a winning pass, because they now needed each other to score.

grounding: A coach sees that sharing a field with unequal roles hardens a rivalry, then uses equal teams, shared goals and the principal's support to reduce it.

passage:
Teacher's note, library period, 18 July. Written by Elizabeth, librarian.
The management combined the English-medium and Kannada-medium Class 9 sections for the library period this term, hoping they would mix. They haven't. There is no shared task; they are only told to read quietly. And the English-medium students were made library monitors, so they check the others' books in and out.
Within a month the monitors call the others slow, and the Kannada-medium group sits by the far window muttering about snobs. Rafiq, a monitor, told me the other side "doesn't even try". Nothing in that room gives him a reason to think otherwise.
Sitting in one room is not the same as meeting.
Next: I've asked the principal to back a joint school newspaper, with mixed teams, equal editor roles for both sections and one deadline everyone must meet. The principal has agreed to announce it at assembly.

qa.q: What role were the English-medium students given in the library?
qa.a: They were made library monitors.

qa.q: How does Rafiq seem to feel about the other group, and why?
qa.a: Rafiq seems to feel superior as a monitor, and with no equal, shared work in the library, that distance has hardened his stereotype.

qa.q: What went wrong with the combined period, and what does Elizabeth propose?
qa.a: There was no shared task and the roles were unequal; Elizabeth proposes a joint newspaper with mixed teams, equal editors, one deadline and the principal's backing.

qa.q: How might the Kannada-medium students experience being checked in and out by monitors?
qa.a: They may feel looked down on and controlled, which pushes them to the far window and to calling the others snobs.

grounding: A librarian notices that putting two sections in one room with no shared goal and unequal roles hardens stereotypes, and plans equal, goal-driven contact backed by the principal.

passage:
Monday, 10 pm
The unity assembly was a mistake, and I planned it. Class 10A and 10B have fought over the cricket ground all year, so I put both sections in the hall for a talk on friendship. 10A, the head boy's section, were made ushers and seated 10B at the back. No task, no reason to speak to each other, only a speech.
By lunch the 10B boys were using "the ushers" as an insult, and someone had scrawled something rude on 10A's board. Worse than before.
Salma, who teaches geography, said over tea, "They were in the same room, but not on the same side. Give them one job they can only finish together, and make them equals."
So: a joint wall map of the town for Founders' Day. Mixed pairs, both sections leading equally. The headmaster has agreed to open it himself.
Chaitanya

qa.q: What did the 10B boys start using as an insult?
qa.a: They started using 'the ushers' as an insult.

qa.q: How does Chaitanya feel about the unity assembly now?
qa.a: Chaitanya feels regretful and responsible, since Chaitanya planned the assembly and it left the two sections worse than before.

qa.q: What is Chaitanya's new plan, and why might it work better?
qa.a: A joint wall map with mixed pairs, equal leadership and the headmaster's support, so the two sections need each other and work as equals.

qa.q: Why might Salma's view of the assembly differ from what Chaitanya first expected?
qa.a: Salma saw that sitting together without a shared goal or equal status doesn't build friendship, while Chaitanya had hoped the talk alone would.

grounding: A teacher sees that seating rival sections together with unequal roles and no shared goal only hardened hostility, and plans equal, cooperative contact backed by the headmaster.
